paras: The killing of Garnett Thompson was the shooting death of a Black man by pursuers in Bayou Sara, West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, on the evening of 11 December 1880, minutes after he shot a white man, J. C. Ball, in a street altercation. A coroner's jury found that he died from "shots fired by unknown hands," and the local paper gave particular attention to a claim that he was an escaped convicted murderer.

According to the Feliciana Sentinel, whose reporter reached the scene minutes later, Ball was walking down Sun street at about 5:30 o'clock when Thompson passed and "in a very defiant manner made some insulting remark." Ball, described as unarmed, struck him; Thompson grappled with him and, as he was tripped and falling, drew a pistol and shot Ball in the left side. While Ball's friends picked him up, others chased the fleeing Thompson for several minutes, and when he was felled he was found to have been shot to death.

The Sentinel added that it had been told that "colored people" who esteemed Ball were among those who fired at Thompson. Ball, attended by Doctors Taylor and Mumford, was not expected to live through the night but was reported out of danger a week later.

Coroner Dr. Chas. Ball held a post-mortem and inquest the next morning, finding eleven gunshot wounds, seven of them to vital parts, and the jury named no one. During the inquest a man from the lower parishes who had stopped off a boat viewed the body and said the dead man was "Thomas Benton," convicted of murder in Thibodeaux Parish and sentenced to hang, who had escaped while being taken to prison. No paper tested that identification, and no report of an arrest or further proceedings appears in the coverage.

The only original account was the Feliciana Sentinel's "A TERRIBLE TRAGEDY." of 18 December, which made the wounding of an "estimable young man" the tragedy and described Thompson's shot as a "bold attempt" on Ball's life. The Louisiana Capitolian of Baton Rouge reprinted the article in full on 23 and 25 December, crediting the Sentinel. The Donaldsonville Chief reduced it to a digest item on 25 December, stating flatly that Thompson "proved to be a murderer who escaped from jail in Terrebonne" and that the jury found he was killed by parties unknown. None of the three papers questioned the killing itself or called for an inquiry beyond the inquest.

reader.title: Killing of Garnett Thompson
bases: An informal party of pursuers chased and shot to death a Black man who had just shot a white man in a street altercation; no officers or deputizing are mentioned, and the coroner's jury named no one (A4, A5, A7).

Every account derives from the Feliciana Sentinel's local report (A3, A4), reprinted in the Louisiana Capitolian (A5, A6) and summarized in the Donaldsonville Chief (A7); no independent report was found.

framing.detail: The Sentinel's 'A TERRIBLE TRAGEDY.' centered the wounded 'estimable young man', called Thompson 'defiant', presented the killing as a pursuit outcome, and stressed his alleged identity as an escaped murderer as a fact 'of peculiar interest'.
The Donaldsonville Chief compressed the story into one digest item noting the pursuit, the escaped-murderer identification and the 'parties unknown' verdict.

conflicts.note: The Sentinel's scan prints 'Garrett' in the identification; the Capitolian reprint prints 'Garnett' throughout. Likely OCR or typesetting variation.

versions.value: Convicted in 'Thibadeaux/Thibodeaux Parish', escaped while being conveyed to prison

conflicts.note: The Chief's digest paraphrases the Sentinel; the Sentinel's longer text is the better evidence.
